pages.text: Nuhu loved Sports Day, but he never won. In the 100 metres, he was always near the back. ‘Medals are for the fast ones,’ he told his friend Ewoenam.
sentences: Nuhu loved Sports Day, but he never won.
In the 100 metres, he was always near the back.
‘Medals are for the fast ones,’ he told his friend Ewoenam.
pages.alt: A boy in a PE kit watches classmates cross a finish line at the back of the pack.

pages.text: Ewoenam shook her head. ‘You never give up, and that counts,’ she said. ‘Let us measure how you improve.’
sentences: Ewoenam shook her head.
‘You never give up, and that counts,’ she said.
‘Let us measure how you improve.’
pages.alt: A girl with a notebook and stopwatch talks earnestly to the boy at the edge of a field.

pages.text: Ewoenam borrowed the PE teacher’s stopwatch. On Monday she timed Nuhu over 100 metres: 21.4 seconds. She wrote it down. ‘That is your starting number,’ she said.
sentences: Ewoenam borrowed the PE teacher’s stopwatch.
On Monday she timed Nuhu over 100 metres: 21.4 seconds.
She wrote it down.
‘That is your starting number,’ she said.
pages.alt: The girl holds a stopwatch as the boy crosses a marked finish line.

pages.text: For three weeks, Nuhu practised starting low and swinging his arms. Ewoenam timed him every Friday. His times went 20.9, 20.3 and then 19.8 seconds.
sentences: For three weeks, Nuhu practised starting low and swinging his arms.
Ewoenam timed him every Friday.
His times went 20.9, 20.3 and then 19.8 seconds.
pages.alt: The boy practises starting crouched on a dirt track while the girl records times.

pages.text: On Sports Day, Nuhu finished sixth out of eight again. There was no medal. But Ewoenam held up the stopwatch. ‘19.7 seconds!’ she shouted. ‘Your fastest ever!’
sentences: On Sports Day, Nuhu finished sixth out of eight again.
There was no medal.
But Ewoenam held up the stopwatch.
‘19.7 seconds!’ she shouted.
‘Your fastest ever!’
pages.alt: The boy crosses the line sixth while the girl cheers and shows the stopwatch.

pages.text: Nuhu felt proud and disappointed at once. ‘Everyone cheered the winners,’ he said. Ewoenam thought. ‘Maybe the prizes should celebrate more than one kind of success.’
sentences: Nuhu felt proud and disappointed at once.
‘Everyone cheered the winners,’ he said.
Ewoenam thought.
‘Maybe the prizes should celebrate more than one kind of success.’
pages.alt: The two friends sit at the side of the track thinking, with ribbons and medals in the background.

pages.text: They took their notebook to the PE teacher, Mr Amankwah. ‘Could we add a Personal Best ribbon?’ they asked. He studied the times. ‘That is a fair idea,’ he said. ‘Let us try it next term.’
sentences: They took their notebook to the PE teacher, Mr Amankwah.
‘Could we add a Personal Best ribbon?’ they asked.
He studied the times.
‘That is a fair idea,’ he said.
‘Let us try it next term.’
pages.alt: The two children show a notebook to a teacher holding a whistle.

pages.text: Next term every child recorded their own time. Nuhu was proud of his ribbon. Some winners were fast, others were improvers, and the best part was that everyone was running. The end.
sentences: Next term every child recorded their own time.
